intro.heading: The plan changed on Tuesday. By Friday, who knows what is different?
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A manager of a small supported living service has just changed how the team supports a man who becomes distressed at busy mealtimes. The team met on Tuesday, talked it through and passed round an easy read sheet. Nobody raised a concern. Three days later the weekend staff arrive, including two who rarely attend meetings, and a relief worker who has never met him. The manager cannot say who has taken in the new approach. It is a worry in any learning disability care service, because the person feels the difference first. Here is how it plays out.

trail.text: The team meets about a changed approach to mealtimes.
Everyone nods. The reasons are explained clearly.
An easy read sheet goes round and the notes are filed.
The weekend team starts. Two were not at the meeting.
A relief worker who has never supported him and relies on a quick handover.
A confident worker who reads the sheet and carries on as before.
Meeting notes and a filed sheet. Nothing showing what each worker understood.
“How do you know your staff support him the agreed way?”

trail_close: The meeting was good and the sheet was clear. What is missing is a quiet way to check, worker by worker, that the approach has landed. The rest of this page shows how.

why.heading: A meeting shows who was there, not who understood
why.sub: A reviewer will not ask who attended. They will ask a worker what they would do.

cards.title: Support is personal
cards.body: In a learning disability service, the right approach differs for each person. A general memory of the training is not enough. Workers need to know what was agreed for this person and why.

cards.title: A meeting reaches only those in it
cards.body: Part time staff, relief workers and night teams often miss the discussion. A sheet in a folder does not show whether anyone has read it or understood it.

cards.title: A short check is gentle
cards.body: A few questions on a phone feel kinder than a test. A wrong answer is treated as a prompt to learn, not a mark against the worker.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: Is CareStream set up for learning disability and autism services?
items.a: Honestly, it is not one of the care settings with its own page on our site. The loop works the same in any service, though, and your own policies, such as positive behaviour support, are what the training is built from. You allocate it in the Training screen and workers complete it in the Staff Hub.

items.q: Is there a CareStream course on learning disability and autism?
items.a: Not as a standalone course in our free CPD library. The Care Certificate course includes a standard on awareness of learning disability and autism. For your own service, you allocate adhoc training on the topic, built from your own policies.

items.q: How would I know whether the team took in a changed approach?
items.a: You allocate short training on the topic after the meeting. Each worker answers on their own phone, and the answers are scored. You can see who understood and who needs another look.

items.q: What happens when someone gets a question wrong?
items.a: It goes into that worker's Follow-up tab and they get an email, at most once a day. They choose Learn & retry, a short lesson then a fresh question, or Just retry the same question. They can retry as often as they need.

items.q: Will the lessons match how we support people?
items.a: Where your policies cover the point, the lesson draws on them, so it teaches what your service does. Where they do not, it falls back on general good practice, which is a useful prompt to improve the policy.

items.q: What do I see across the team?
items.a: The Knowledge gaps view shows open gaps, staff affected, the questions most often missed and the weakest topics. A digest email arrives on Monday. Nothing alerts you each time someone gets a question wrong.

items.q: Does this replace our own training for supporting a person?
items.a: No. Knowing a person well, shadowing and observed practice cannot be done on a phone. CareStream checks understanding of what was agreed and keeps the record, alongside the supervision and shadowing you already do.

faqs.heading: Learning disability training and CareStream, answered

items.q: What is learning disability training for care staff?
items.a: It helps workers understand how to support people with a learning disability and autistic people, including communication, person centred planning and positive behaviour support. The best versions combine learning with practice. CareStream adds a follow up check, built from your own policies.

There is no standalone autism course in the free CPD library. The Care Certificate course includes a standard on awareness of learning disability and autism. You can also allocate adhoc training on the topic from your own policies, to check that a team has understood your approach.

items.q: What if a worker gets a question wrong?
items.a: It appears in their Follow-up tab. They can choose Learn & retry, a short lesson followed by a fresh question, or Just retry the same question, as often as they need. Treat it as information, not failure.

items.q: Can I use it for learning disability care in supported living?
items.a: Yes. It works the same in supported living, residential and community services. Workers use the Staff Hub on their own phone, so a relief or weekend worker is checked as well as the core team.

items.q: How soon after a team meeting should the check go out?
items.a: Within a few days is sensible: early enough that the meeting is fresh, late enough to show what stuck. You choose when to allocate it, and you can set a due date.
No. Practical support and communication need observation by someone who knows the person. Pair a knowledge check with face to face sessions and supervision.

items.q: What does the law say about learning disability and autism training?
items.a: Skills for Care says all CQC registered providers must ensure staff have training on learning disability and autism, appropriate to their role, under the Health and Care Act 2022. The CQC page on training staff to support autistic people and people with a learning disability explains what it expects.

items.q: What does CQC expect providers to show?
items.a: CQC says it expects providers to assess each person's training needs, keep a record if someone is judged not to need the training, monitor how effective training is, and check staff are competent and applying what they learned. A record of questions, lessons and results is one way to show the last two.

guide.heading: A practical way to follow up a change in how you support someone
guide.lede: Learning disability training does not end with the session or the meeting. The follow up is where a manager learns whether the approach reached the whole team, including the people who were not in the room.

sections.h3: Why the follow up matters for CQC
paragraphs: The CQC guidance on training staff to support autistic people and people with a learning disability says it expects providers to monitor how effective their training is, and to check that staff are competent and applying what they learned. A signature on a meeting sheet does not show either.

This applies to the training you buy and to the learning you do in house, such as a changed support plan. CareStream does not decide what your staff need. It gives you a record of what each person was asked, what they got wrong and whether the gap closed.

sections.h3: Four checks that fit a busy service
checklist: Within a week: allocate short training on the topic of the meeting, and set a due date
Include relief, part time and night workers, not just the core team
Look at the Knowledge gaps view and the Monday digest, and note any question most people missed
Pair it with a short conversation or observed shift for anyone still unsure

paragraphs: Tell the team why you are checking. In learning disability care, the person feels the difference when a worker gets it wrong, and workers want to get it right. Say the questions are there to help, not to catch anyone out. For a deeper review of restrictive practice, see the positive behaviour support audit, and for health checks the health action plan audit. Our blog on who needs retraining helps decide who to include.
